title: Packages, Bundling, and Vite
summary: Install packages with npm, see why browsers need your code bundled, run a site with Vite's dev server, and build it into small, hashed files.
intro: So far you've written every file by hand and served the folder as it is. Real projects aren't built that way. They lean on code other people wrote and shared, often thousands of files of it, and a browser can't load that code the way it sits on your disk. This lesson builds a small notes page, one step at a time, the way teams work today. You'll install a package with npm, the tool every JavaScript project uses to get shared code. You'll see why the browser can't use that package as it is, and what a bundler does about it. Then you'll run the page with Vite, which serves your site while you work, and build it into the few small files that go online. React, and every framework after it, is installed and run exactly this way.

steps.title: Packages and npm
steps.body:
Some problems have been solved thousands of times: formatting dates, drawing charts, showing maps, taking payments. Writing your own every time is slow, and the result usually has bugs the shared versions fixed years ago. So developers publish their code as packages, and npm is how JavaScript developers get them. Every tool in the rest of this course, Vite and Tailwind included, and React after it, arrives this way, so this part starts from nothing.

## Packages and the registry

A **package** is a folder of code someone has published for others to use, with a name, a version number, and a file called `package.json` that describes it. The **npm registry**, at npmjs.com, is a public library of millions of packages, free to download.

**npm** is the program that downloads them. It came with **Node.js**, the program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, which you installed with Hack University. The name started out as short for Node Package Manager. You use it in the terminal.

Here's the plan for this lesson. You'll make a small notes page that shows how long ago each note was written, like 3 days ago. Working that out by hand means counting hours and days and getting the plurals right, and a popular package called **date-fns** already does it.

## Your project's package.json

A **project** is a folder with its own `package.json` at the top. Make a folder called `my-app` in the Playground, move the terminal into it with `cd my-app`, and run `npm init -y`, which writes a starter `package.json` (the `-y` says yes to every default question). Run the two installs in the examples below, then tidy the file to match this one:

```json
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "date-fns": "^4.4.0"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "vite": "^8.3.8"
  }
}
```

- `name` and `version` identify the project.
- `"private": true` stops npm from ever publishing it to the registry by accident.
- `"type": "module"` says this project's JavaScript files use `import` and `export`, the modules from the JavaScript lessons.
- `scripts` names commands you run often. The next parts use all three.

## Versions

Packages are numbered with **semantic versioning**: three numbers, major.minor.patch. A new **patch** (4.4.1) only fixes bugs. A new **minor** version (4.5.0) adds features without breaking anything. A new **major** version (5.0.0) may break code that worked with the old one. The `^` in `^4.4.0` means 4.4.0 or any newer 4.x, so you get fixes and features, but never a breaking change by surprise.

## Two kinds of dependencies

- **dependencies** are code your page uses when it runs. date-fns ends up inside the files your visitors download.
- **devDependencies** are tools you only use while you build, and they never reach the browser. Vite is one. Install them with `npm install -D`, short for `--save-dev`.

## node_modules and the lockfile

```diagram packages-and-bundling-npm-install
npm install reads your list, downloads from the registry, and writes two things.
```

In the diagram, `npm install` reads `package.json` (step 1), downloads each package from the registry, along with the packages it needs and the ones those need (step 2), and writes what it got into your project (step 3). The code goes in a folder called `node_modules`. Installing Vite brought 14 other packages with it. You never edit anything in there. You also leave it out of **version control**, the system that keeps the history of a project's files so a team can share them (usually git, which the React course sets up), and you never send it to anyone. It's big, 57 MB for this project, and anyone can rebuild it by running `npm install` with no package name, which reads `package.json` and downloads everything listed.

`package-lock.json` is the **lockfile**. It records the exact version of every package in `node_modules`, where it was downloaded from, and a **hash** of its contents: a short fingerprint worked out from the file's bytes, which comes out different if even one byte changes. `^4.4.0` allows many versions, and the lockfile says which one you actually got, so everyone on your team, and the computer that builds your site, installs exactly the same code. Keep it next to `package.json`, and put both in version control.

## Scripts and npx

`npm run` and a script's name runs that script: `npm run build` runs the command that `build` holds. Inside a script, npm finds the commands your packages install, like `vite`, in `node_modules/.bin`. To run one of those without a script, use `npx`, as in `npx vite`. The first lessons used `npx` to run a server package the same way.

## A word on trust

Installing a package runs code strangers wrote, on your computer and later in your visitors' browsers. Prefer packages many people use and that were updated recently. The `found 0 vulnerabilities` line comes from **npm audit**, which checks what you installed against a public list of known security problems.

examples.title: Installing date-fns
examples.prompt: In the `my-app` folder, install the package the notes page needs.
examples.output:
added 1 package, and audited 2 packages in 465ms

1 package is looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

found 0 vulnerabilities
examples.explanation: `added 1 package` means npm downloaded date-fns into `node_modules`, and since date-fns needs no other packages, that's all. Audited 2 packages counts what npm checked for known security problems: date-fns and your own project. The funding lines say the package's authors accept donations, and `npm fund` lists where. Your time will differ. Open `package.json` and you'll find a new `dependencies` entry, `"date-fns": "^4.4.0"`, and a new `package-lock.json` next to it. Your version number may be higher, since npm installs the newest one.

examples.title: Installing Vite as a dev tool
examples.prompt: Vite builds the page but never runs in it, so it goes in devDependencies. `-D` is short for `--save-dev`.
examples.output:
added 15 packages, and audited 17 packages in 589ms

9 packages are looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

found 0 vulnerabilities
examples.explanation: This time npm added 15 packages: Vite, and the 14 it needs, like Rolldown, its bundler, and Lightning CSS, which reads and shrinks stylesheets. Some of them are written in Rust for speed, so npm picked the copy built for your kind of computer. All of them land in `node_modules`, and only `vite` gets a line in `package.json`, under `devDependencies`. The lockfile records the other 14, so the next `npm install` on another computer brings exactly the same ones. With the `scripts` from the body added to `package.json`, the project is ready for the next part.

steps.title: Why we bundle
steps.body:
With date-fns installed, you'd expect to import it the way the JavaScript lessons imported your own modules. Try it, and the page breaks. Why it breaks, and what it costs to fix by hand, is the reason bundlers exist. ## The notes page The page itself is `index.html`, at the top of the project, next to `package.json`: ```html Notes

Notes

    ``` Your own code goes in a folder called `src`, short for source. `src/notes.js` holds the notes, each with the time it was written: ```javascript const hoursAgo = (hours) => new Date(Date.now() - hours * 60 * 60 * 1000); export const notes = [ { text: "Buy milk", createdAt: hoursAgo(2) }, { text: "Call the dentist", createdAt: hoursAgo(26) }, { text: "Read about bundlers", createdAt: hoursAgo(72) }, ]; ``` `Date.now()` is the time now, in milliseconds, and `new Date()` turns a number of milliseconds into a date, an object that stands for one moment in time. So `hoursAgo(2)` is the moment two hours ago. `src/style.css` sets a font and some spacing, and `src/help.js` exports a `showHelp` function that opens a small dialog. `src/main.js` ties them together, and example 1 shows it: it imports the package, the notes, and the stylesheet, and puts the notes on the page. ## Bare imports Look at the first import, `from "date-fns"`. That's a **bare specifier**: a package's name, not a path. Node.js knows to look for names like that in `node_modules`. A browser only knows URLs, and a name without `/`, `./`, or `../` in front isn't one. Serve the folder with Python's server, open the page, and the list stays empty while the console shows this error: ```text TypeError: Failed to resolve module specifier "date-fns". Relative references must start with either "/", "./", or "../". ``` The stylesheet import has a problem too: browsers import JavaScript modules, and a CSS file isn't one. ## Import maps Browsers do have a fix for names: an **import map**, a small block of JSON in the page that says which URL each name stands for (example 2). With one in place, the notes appear. Now open the Network panel and count. To show three notes, the browser made 307 requests. The main file of date-fns imports each of its 300 or so functions from a file of its own, so the browser fetched 304 files from the package, though the page uses one function. That's the trouble with sending modules as they are: - **Many requests.** Even over HTTP/2's shared connection, every file costs something to ask for, track, and store. - **A waterfall.** The browser only learns what a module imports after downloading it. A chain five imports deep costs five round trips, one after another. On a phone with 100 ms round trips, that's half a second of waiting before any of it runs. - **Dead weight.** Everything the package's main file imports gets downloaded, whether the page uses it or not. ## What a bundler does A **bundler** is a tool that reads your code before it goes online and rewrites it into a few files that load fast. It starts from an **entry**, here `index.html`, and follows every import to build the **module graph**: every file the page needs, and which file imports which. Then it does three jobs: 1. **Resolve.** Turn every import into a real file. For `"date-fns"`, that means finding the package in `node_modules` and reading its `package.json` to learn which file is its entry. 2. **Transform.** Turn anything browsers can't load into something they can. The CSS import becomes a real stylesheet. In the React course, the same step turns JSX, which is HTML written inside JavaScript, and TypeScript, which is JavaScript with types added, into plain JavaScript. 3. **Combine.** Join the modules into a few files, called **bundles** or **chunks**, and leave out the code nothing uses. ```diagram packages-and-bundling-module-graph The module graph on the left becomes two files on the right. ``` On the left of the diagram is the module graph: your three files, and a package with hundreds of its own. On the right, it's two files the browser can load in one round trip: one JavaScript bundle and one stylesheet. ## The tools webpack made bundling the normal way to build in the 2010s, and you'll still find it in older projects. Rollup, Parcel, and esbuild came after. **Vite**, French for quick and said veet, is the usual choice for new projects today, and it's what this course and the React course use. Since version 8, Vite bundles with **Rolldown**, a fast bundler written in the Rust language. The next two parts show what Vite does while you work, and then what it does when you build.

examples.title: The notes page's main module
examples.prompt: `src/main.js` in the `my-app` project, the module that `index.html` loads. It fills the empty list with the notes, and loads the help only when it's needed.
examples.explanation: The first import is the bare one: a package name. The second is a relative path to your own file, which exports an array of notes, each with its text and the `Date` it was written. The third imports a stylesheet for what it does, not for a value, which only works with a bundler. The loop is the DOM code you know: for each note, make a list item and put in its text, then how long ago it was written. `formatDistanceToNow` turns a date into words like about 2 hours ago, and `addSuffix: true` adds the ago. The last lines load `help.js` only when someone clicks the button. That `import()` with parentheses comes back in the build part, where it decides how the files get split.

examples.title: Naming a package with an import map
examples.prompt: The same page, fixed without a bundler. The import map has to come before any module that uses the names it defines. The CSS import was taken out of `main.js` for this test, since browsers can't import it.
examples.explanation: `type="importmap"` holds JSON, not code. Each key under `imports` is a name your modules use, and its value is the URL to load in its place. Now when `main.js` asks for `"date-fns"`, the browser loads `/node_modules/date-fns/index.js`, a file Python's server can send. It works in every current browser. Import maps are a fine choice for a small page with a package or two, and for loading packages with no build step from a CDN, a service that keeps copies of files on servers around the world, which the next lesson explains. But this one turned one import into 304 requests, because `index.js` imports every function in the package. A bundler would have sent only what the page uses, in one file.

steps.title: Vite while you work
steps.body:
While you build a page, you save a file dozens of times an hour and want to see each change at once. Older bundlers rebuilt the whole bundle on every save, which on a big app took seconds each time. Vite takes a different route: while you work, it doesn't bundle your own code at all.

## The dev server

The `dev` script in `package.json` runs `vite`, so `npm run dev` starts Vite's **dev server**: a server on localhost that serves your project while you work on it (example 1). Open the address it prints, and the notes appear, each with its age. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.

## Native modules, prepared on request

Vite sends your files to the browser as separate modules, the way the browser loads them anyway, and does each file's work at the moment the browser asks for it. On localhost a request takes almost no time, so many small files cost little. Open the Network panel and count again: the page, your three files, Vite's own script, and a single file for date-fns. Seven requests, where the import map made 307.

Two things happened to your files on the way:

- **Imports are rewritten.** Ask Vite for `/src/main.js` and its first line comes back as `import { formatDistanceToNow } from "/node_modules/.vite/deps/date-fns.js?v=bf340a72"`, a real path the browser can fetch.
- **Files are transformed.** `/src/style.css` comes back as JavaScript that adds the stylesheet to the page, which is how the CSS import works.

## Dependency pre-bundling

That `.vite/deps` path comes from **dependency pre-bundling**. The first time the dev server starts, Vite finds the packages your code imports and bundles each one into a single file in `node_modules/.vite/deps`, using Rolldown. That's how 304 files from date-fns became one. Packages almost never change while you work, so Vite does this once, reuses it, and redoes it only when you install something new. On the way, it also converts packages written in **CommonJS**, the older `require` style of modules that Node.js started with, into modules the browser understands.

## Hot module replacement

Vite's script, `/@vite/client`, keeps a WebSocket open to the dev server, the two-way connection from the lesson on fetch and other Web APIs. When you save a file, the server tells the page what changed, and the page takes in the new code without you pressing reload. That's **hot module replacement**, or HMR.

- Save a CSS file, and the new styles replace the old ones in place. Nothing reloads, so the scroll position and whatever you typed in a form stay put.
- Save a JavaScript file that doesn't say how to swap itself in, and Vite reloads the whole page.

Frameworks add that missing piece, which is why in the React course, a component you edit updates in place, and keeps its data. Example 1 shows both kinds of update in the terminal.

## Ports and the proxy

Vite's settings go in `vite.config.js`, at the top of the project (example 2). Two of them come up often.

**The port.** Vite starts on port 5173. Recall address already in use from the lesson on how the browser reaches a server: only one program can listen on a port. When 5173 is taken, Vite doesn't stop, it quietly takes the next free port, like 5174, which is what happened in example 1. That's handy until a second copy of your app sits on 5174 and you keep testing the old one on 5173. `strictPort: true` makes Vite stop with Port 5173 is already in use instead.

**The proxy.** Your page runs at `http://localhost:5173` and the backend it calls, like the notes server from the fetch lesson, might run at `http://localhost:8000`. Recall from the fetch lesson that another port means another origin, so the browser won't let your code read the backend's answers unless the backend sends CORS headers. A **proxy** sidesteps that: your page fetches `/api/notes` from its own origin, and Vite passes the request on to the backend and hands back the answer. The browser only ever talks to one origin. The proxy only exists while `npm run dev` runs, so in production the real server or your host does the same job, or the backend allows your origin with CORS.

## The short way to start

You built this project by hand to see every piece. At work, `npm create vite@latest`, where `@latest` asks for the newest version, asks a few questions and writes the folder, `package.json`, and starter files for you. The React course starts its project that way.

examples.title: Running the dev server, then saving changes
examples.prompt: In the `my-app` folder, start the dev server and open the address it prints. Then change the margin in `src/style.css` and save, and change a note's text in `src/notes.js` and save. This is everything the terminal printed.
examples.output:
> my-app@1.0.0 dev
> vite

Port 5173 is in use, trying another one...

  VITE v8.3.8  ready in 55 ms

  ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5174/
  ➜  Network: use --host to expose
1:27:08 PM [vite] (client) hmr update /src/style.css
1:27:09 PM [vite] (client) page reload src/notes.js
examples.explanation: The two lines starting with `>` are npm saying which script it ran and the command inside it. On the computer this ran on, another dev server already had port 5173, so Vite said so and took 5174. On yours, it will most likely say 5173. ready in 55 ms is how long the server took to start, since it bundles nothing of yours up front. Network: use --host to expose means it listens on localhost alone, so nobody else on your Wi-Fi can reach it. The last two lines are the saves. `hmr update /src/style.css` means the new styles were swapped into the open page. `page reload src/notes.js` means Vite reloaded the page, since that file has no way to swap itself in.

examples.title: Setting the port and a proxy
examples.prompt: `vite.config.js`, next to `package.json`. It pins the port and sends API requests on to a backend running on port 8000.
examples.explanation: `defineConfig` does nothing but hand back the object you give it. It's there so your editor knows which settings exist and can suggest them as you type. Everything under `server` is for the dev server. `port` picks the port, and `strictPort: true` turns quietly moving to the next one into an error. Under `proxy`, each key is the start of a path: any request whose path starts with `/api`, like `fetch("/api/notes")` from your page, is sent on to `http://localhost:8000/api/notes`, and the backend's answer comes back as if Vite had sent it. Everything else is served by Vite as before. Restart the dev server after changing this file so it reads the new settings.

steps.title: The production build
steps.body:
The dev server is built for your own computer: hundreds of small files, nothing shrunk, all of it prepared on request. Over a real network to a phone, that would be slow. So before a site goes online, you **build** it: Vite bundles everything into a few small files that any web server can send.

## Building

`npm run build` runs `vite build` (example 1). Rolldown starts from `index.html`, follows the module graph, and writes the result into a folder called `dist`, short for distribution. It prints each file with its size, and its size after gzip, a way of compressing files that the next lesson explains. The gzip size is close to what will really travel over the network.

312 modules went in, and three files came out, plus a new `index.html`. Here's what happened on the way.

## Tree shaking

The date-fns folder in `node_modules` holds 26 MB in 1,428 JavaScript files, with translations into 96 languages. The page's JavaScript bundle, your code included, is 12.31 kB. Vite kept the one function the page imports and the few helpers it needs, and left the rest out. Leaving out code that nothing uses is called **tree shaking**: shake the module graph, and the dead leaves fall off.

It works because `import` and `export` are written plainly in the code, so a bundler can tell which names each file uses without running anything. It also has to know that a file does nothing just by being loaded, and date-fns says so in its `package.json` with `"sideEffects": false`. A package that sets things up the moment it loads, like adding click handlers to the page, can't be shaken as well, and the Bootstrap lesson shows one.

## Minification

Then **minification** rewrites the code as small as it can while doing exactly the same thing: it removes spaces, line breaks, and comments, shortens names nothing outside uses, and picks shorter ways to write values. The notes page's eight-line stylesheet came out as one line:

```css
body{margin:2rem;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif}li{padding:.25rem 0}
```

## Code splitting

`main.js` loads the help text with `import("./help.js")`, the function form of import, which waits until that line runs. Vite puts each file loaded that way in a chunk of its own, here `help-Q_Mjzo9I.js`, and the browser only downloads it when someone presses Show help. That's **code splitting**. Splitting off what most visitors never use, like a settings page, a chart, or a text editor, keeps the first download small. Splitting everything is no good either, since each chunk is another request.

## Content hashes

Each file name has a code in it, like `COKNwWg4`. That's a **content hash**, the kind of fingerprint the lockfile keeps, worked out from the file's contents. Change the file, and the hash changes. Leave it alone, and the hash stays the same build after build, as example 2 shows. The built `index.html` points at the hashed names, so every build that changes a file gives it a new name, and a browser can never mix an old file with a new one.

```diagram packages-and-bundling-build
Your files on the left, and what vite build writes into dist on the right.
```

In the diagram, your four source files and the package become three hashed files in `dist/assets`, and a new `index.html` that points at them. The next lesson shows how those names let browsers keep the files for a year.

## Source maps

Minified code is unreadable, so an error in it would point at line 1, character 9,000. A **source map** is a file that links each spot in the built code back to your own file and line. Build with `npx vite build --sourcemap` and each bundle gets a `.map` file next to it, which DevTools loads to show your own code in errors and while you step through it. Source maps also show your code to anyone who looks, so some teams send them only to an error-tracking service instead of putting them online.

## Checking the build

`npm run preview` serves the `dist` folder at `http://localhost:4173`, so you can click through the built site before anyone else sees it. It's for checking only, not for running a real site. Putting the site online, called **deploying**, means copying `dist` to a host that serves files, like Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, or GitHub Pages, or to a server of your own.

Your hashes will differ, since they come from your files' contents.

examples.title: A changed file gets a new name
examples.prompt: Change Buy milk to Buy oat milk in `src/notes.js` and build again. Compare the four files with example 1.
examples.output:
> my-app@1.0.0 build
> vite build

vite v8.3.8 building client environment for production...
transforming...
✓ 312 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
computing gzip size...
dist/index.html                  0.48 kB │ gzip: 0.29 kB
dist/assets/index-lc8mfrVt.css   0.07 kB │ gzip: 0.09 kB
dist/assets/help-Q_Mjzo9I.js     0.24 kB │ gzip: 0.20 kB
dist/assets/index-BBx9I6BA.js   12.31 kB │ gzip: 4.49 kB

examples.explanation: Only one name changed: the main bundle went from `index-COKNwWg4.js` to `index-BBx9I6BA.js`, because the notes are inside it. The stylesheet and the help chunk kept their names, since not a byte of them changed. `index.html` kept its name too, as it must, but its contents now point at the new bundle. So a visitor who already has the stylesheet and the help chunk keeps using them, and only downloads the one file that's new. Change the note back and build again, and the old name, `index-COKNwWg4.js`, comes back: the hash depends only on what's in the file.

recap:
- A package is shared code with a name and a version, and npm installs it from the npm registry.
- package.json lists your packages and scripts, node_modules holds their code, and the lockfile pins exact versions.
- dependencies run in the page, devDependencies are tools for building, and node_modules stays out of version control.
- Browsers can't resolve a bare import like date-fns, and loading a package's modules one by one is slow.
- A bundler follows the module graph from an entry, then resolves, transforms, and combines it into a few files.
- Vite's dev server serves your files as native modules, pre-bundles packages, and swaps in changes with HMR.
- vite build tree-shakes, minifies, and splits your code into files in dist whose names change only when their contents do.
